content:
Islam, the critic says, has always been hostile to the Jews and to their worship. The charge is repeated in a familiar question, "Why do Muslims hate Jews?", which assumes its own answer.

This article aims to provide context to that charge, insha'Allah, by looking at synagogues: what the Quran says of them, what the Prophet did, and what one synagogue under Muslim rule preserved.

The Quran sets the rule at the moment it first permits fighting: had God not repelled some people by others, "there would surely have been pulled down monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques, in which the name of Allah is commemorated in abundant measure" (22:40).[1]

Verse 22:40 names four kinds of house and joins them in one clause: places "in which the name of Allah is commemorated in abundant measure". Synagogues stand in the list before the mosque.

The verse gives the reason the Muslims were allowed to defend themselves at all. The protection of other people's worship is part of the purpose of the permission.

Strength: firm. The Quran's first word on war protects the synagogue.

In Medina the Jews had a house of study, the bayt al-midras. Abu Hurayra reports that the Prophet (peace be upon him) went there with his companions and spoke to its people.[2]

He went to their house to address them in it. Whatever the dispute between them, the place of their study was a place he visited.

The Ben Ezra Synagogue stands in Fustat, Old Cairo. Documents found in it show that it existed before 882, and it was probably older still.[3]

Its storeroom, the geniza, received worn-out writings for about 850 years: letters, contracts, court records and scripture. Solomon Schechter brought most of them to Cambridge University Library in the 1890s.[4]

Those papers are the fullest record of any medieval Jewish community, and the community they record lived, traded and prayed in a Muslim city.

Moses Maimonides, the greatest Jewish legal scholar of the Middle Ages, became head of the Jews of Egypt in 1171 and worshipped at the Ben Ezra Synagogue. Documents in his own hand survive among the Geniza papers.[5]

He wrote his legal code and the Guide for the Perplexed in that city, and served as a physician at the court of Saladin's family.

The record has a breach, and we name it. Around 1013 the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim ordered the destruction of the churches and synagogues of his domains, and the Ben Ezra Synagogue was pulled down.[6]

It was rebuilt, and it stands today. His order broke the rule of 22:40.

Islamic law protects what the Quran protects. "There is no compulsion in religion" (2:256).

The bottom line

The Quran names synagogues among the houses of God and makes their protection part of the reason for fighting. The Prophet visited the Jews' house of study. A synagogue in Cairo kept 850 years of Jewish life under Muslim rule, and Maimonides prayed in it.

One ruler broke the rule, and his order was reversed. The charge of permanent hostility has to set aside the Quran, the hadith and the Geniza to stand.

Notes

  1. Quran 22:40. The word for synagogues is salawat; the Quranic Arabic Corpus lists the verse as the Quran's one reference to synagogues.
  2. Sahih al-Bukhari 6944 and 7348, report of Abu Hurayra.
  3. Wikipedia, "Ben Ezra Synagogue", citing the evidence of the Geniza documents.
  4. Wikipedia, "Cairo Geniza".
  5. Wikipedia, "Ben Ezra Synagogue", on Maimonides as nagid.
  6. Smarthistory, "Ben Ezra Synagogue, Fustat, Egypt".
